analysis.one_liner: Restores Clean Water Act protections for streams and wetlands stripped by a 2020 rule, and directs regulators to write a science-based replacement.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it sat in a Transportation and Infrastructure subcommittee from May 2020 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the 2020 rule it targeted remained in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2020 the Trump administration finalized a rule that narrowed which streams, lakes, and wetlands count as "waters of the United States" under the Clean Water Act, removing federal pollution protections from waters that had been covered since 1986. This bill would wipe out that rule and require the EPA and Army Corps of Engineers to write a new definition within two years, based on the best available science, covering waters that feed drinking supplies for roughly 117 million Americans. The bill never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who drink from or live downstream of the streams and wetlands the 2020 rule left unprotected — about 117 million Americans get drinking water from these systems. Also downstream communities facing pollution, flooding, and higher drinking-water treatment costs, the $887 billion outdoor recreation economy, and municipal water systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downstream residents, water utilities, outdoor businesses

how_it_helps.text: Nullifies the 2020 Navigable Waters Protection Rule, which the bill's findings say eliminated federal protections on 18 to 71 percent of the nation's stream and river miles and over half of the wetlands in the continental United States. [S3]

Requires EPA and the Army Corps to write a new definition within two years that covers waters affecting the integrity of navigable and interstate waters, and that prevents any degradation of surface water quality, any increase in drinking-water contaminants, any added flood risk, and any disproportionate harm to minority or low-income communities. [S2] [S3]

Restores federal oversight over roughly 16,000 permitted facilities — industrial plants and sewage systems — that the bill says could discharge pollutants without Clean Water Act permits under the 2020 rule. [S3]

Protects the intermittent and ephemeral streams that make up more than two-thirds of all streams in the lower 48 states and feed public drinking water systems serving approximately 117 million Americans. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Industrial dischargers, land developers, and some farm operations that gained freedom from federal permitting when the 2020 rule narrowed coverage; they would again need Clean Water Act permits and face pollution limits. Compliance costs could ultimately show up in the prices of goods and development.
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial polluters, developers, some farm operations

drawbacks.text: A broader federal jurisdiction means more permitting, paperwork, and compliance costs for farmers, landowners, and small developers who found the 2020 rule's clearer, narrower definition easier to work with — a real cost the bill does not compensate. [S2]

The bill requires implementation of the Clean Water Act to prevent "any" degradation of surface water quality, a stricter standard than the Act's own terms, which could generate litigation and regulatory uncertainty. [S3]

Overriding an agency rule by statute, rather than through the normal regulatory process, settles the question for one Congress and invites the next administration to reopen it — the definition has already bounced between administrations since 2015. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — restoring pollution and flood protection to waters that supply drinking water to a third of the country — is large and grounded in the EPA's own science review, which the bill's findings quote. The costs fall on dischargers and land developers in the form of permits and limits, and partly on landowners who face renewed paperwork. The bill is aggressively drafted: the no-exception 'prevent any degradation' standard and the two-year rewrite deadline would strain the agencies and likely be challenged. On balance, restoring protections that existed for decades under both parties outweighs the compliance costs, though the drafting invites disputes.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources and Environment subcommittee, never received a markup or floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio, joined by Rep. Grace Napolitano, introduced the bill on May 8, 2020 to nullify the Navigable Waters Protection Rule finalized weeks earlier. [S1] [S3]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced. [S5]
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, where it remained; no further action was taken. [S5]
Eighty-six House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did. [S4]
With no markup or vote, the 2020 rule the bill targeted stayed in force through the end of the 116th Congress. [S5] [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The industries the 2020 rule freed from federal permitting — industrial facilities that can discharge into newly unprotected streams and wetlands, and developers building on former wetlands — came out ahead, along with the Trump administration, which achieved its regulatory narrowing. Roughly 117 million people whose drinking water comes from those waters bear the residual risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial dischargers, developers, and the Trump EPA

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee, which never marked it up.

for.name: Rep. Grace Napolitano
for.role: Original cosponsor; Chair, Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Joined DeFazio in introducing the bill.

against.name: Trump administration EPA and Army Corps
against.role: Agencies that finalized the Navigable Waters Protection Rule
against.what_they_did: Finalized and implemented the 2020 rule the bill sought to nullify; the rule took effect while the bill sat in subcommittee.

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the support needed to advance past the committee stage.

sides.party_line_note: All 86 cosponsors were Democrats and no House Republican signed on, though the bill never got far enough to produce a recorded vote; the bill text itself frames the fight as overturning a Trump-era rule that cut back Reagan-era protections. [S4] [S3]

industries.industry: Industrial polluters and dischargers (manufacturing, energy, sewage treatment)
industries.note: The bill restores Clean Water Act permitting for roughly 16,000 facilities that the 2020 rule allowed to discharge without federal oversight. Those discharges flow into the drinking-water sources and recreation waters of downstream communities. [S3]

A broad waters definition means wetlands fill permits and mitigation requirements that the 2020 rule had removed, raising the cost of building on former wetlands. Developers were among the main backers of the narrowed rule. [S2]

Most national farm groups supported the 2020 rule's narrower jurisdiction, which spared many ditches and isolated wetlands from permitting; the bill restores that regulatory exposure. At the same time, the bill's findings emphasize that farm communities depend on clean, reliable water sources the rule leaves unprotected. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Outdoor recreation economy ($887 billion: hunting, fishing, wildlife-watching)
industries.note: The bill's findings tie this economy directly to access to clean water and aquatic habitat; restoring protections for streams and wetlands protects the fish, waterfowl, and recreation it depends on. [S3]

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and drinking-water systems
industries.note: Protecting upstream streams lowers contamination and flood risk at the source, cutting the cost of treating drinking water — the Trump administration's own economic analysis acknowledged increased treatment and reservoir maintenance costs under the rule. [S3]
